name: Gradual tanning lotion

lead: A gradual tanning lotion is a moisturizer or body lotion that contains a small amount of a self-tanning agent, usually dihydroxyacetone (DHA). Applied regularly, it deepens skin colour step by step rather than in one dark application.
Proponents like it because slow build-up is less likely to leave streaks or an orange cast than a one-off self-tan. It is not a sunscreen and has not been tested in published appearance trials.

paras: DHA is a simple sugar that reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a Maillard (browning) reaction. The brown pigments produced are not melanin and form without UV light. They fade over several days as the outer skin sheds, which is why gradual products are reapplied.

Reported concerns centre on DHA rather than on lotions in particular: contact dermatitis, a possible increase in free-radical formation in sun-exposed skin soon after application, and a lack of meaningful UV protection. Regulators approve DHA for external use and not for the eyes, lips or mucous membranes.

web.title: Tan Son Nhut Air Base — Wikipedia

lead: A gradual tanning lotion, also called a build-up tanner, is a lotion or moisturizer that contains a mild self-tanning agent so that colour deepens with repeated daily use.[1] Encyclopedic sources say a slight change in skin colour is usually visible after the first application and darkens with more frequent use.[1]

The most common active ingredient in sunless tanners is dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a three-carbon sugar that stains the outer skin layer through a browning (Maillard) reaction rather than by stimulating melanin.[1][2] Drugstore self-tanners typically contain 3 to 5 percent DHA, with higher concentrations in professional products.[1][2] Gradual lotions are generally formulated with less colour per application, though specific concentrations are not given in the sources reviewed.
No clinical studies of gradual tanning lotions as appearance products have been published in the sources reviewed. Safety discussion centres on DHA more broadly.
infobox: Within hours; deepens over 24 to 72 hours and with repeated use[1][2]
DHA gives an SPF of about 3 per one summary[2]
DHA approved in the US for external use only[1]

paras: Sunless tanning is divided into several categories: temporary bronzers, DHA self-tanners, spray tans, tanning pills and injectable products.[1] Gradual lotions are described as a recent trend in which a moisturizer carries a small dose of tanning agent for use over multiple days.[1]

Products are sold as body lotions and as facial moisturizers. Some blend DHA with erythrulose, a related sugar that develops colour more slowly.[1] Patent filings have also described formulations that combine tanning agents with natural plant pigments.[3]

The skin-browning effect of DHA was first noticed in the 1920s by German scientists, and Eva Wittgenstein later observed it in the 1950s while studying children treated orally with DHA at Cincinnati.[2][1] Man-Tan was the first commercial DHA self-tanner in 1959, followed by Coppertone's Quick Tan in 1960; both were criticised for orange colour and streaking.[1][2]
Reformulations in the 1980s and 1990s produced more natural shades, and gradual products came later as a way to lessen streaking and uneven colour.[1][2]

DHA reacts with amino acid residues in keratin in the stratum corneum, forming brown compounds called melanoidins that resemble melanin in colour but arise without UV light and without involving melanocytes.[1][2] The colour begins to appear in 2 to 4 hours and fades as the outer cells are shed.[2]

No studies found. Laboratory work on DHA has reported effects in cultured skin cells, including DNA damage and cell-cycle arrest in keratinocytes, and a study of skin samples reported increased free-radical formation after DHA application followed by sun exposure; these findings come from cell and tissue experiments and are debated.[1]

The US Food and Drug Administration approves DHA for application to the external skin and not for use around the eyes, on the lips or on mucous membranes.[1] DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis, and fragrance in tanning lotions can trigger allergic or asthma reactions.[1]

A fake tan does not protect against UV. Some summaries state that DHA gives an SPF of about 3, and that free-radical formation in treated skin rose after sun exposure within about 24 hours of application.[1][2] An FDA-cited estimate in one summary says roughly 11 percent of applied DHA may reach living skin layers.[2]

In looksmaxxing forums, tanning is discussed mainly alongside tinted moisturizers, BB creams and bronzers as a way to look healthier and even out skin tone; forum users say these products give a more natural look than heavier foundation.[4] Gradual lotions as such are rarely discussed by name in the threads reviewed, so community views specific to them are not documented here.

timeline.event: Eva Wittgenstein observes skin browning from DHA in children treated at Cincinnati.[1]
Man-Tan becomes the first commercial DHA self-tanner.[1]
Coppertone launches its Quick Tan DHA product.[1]
The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety issues an opinion that DHA spray tanning poses no risk, which specialists criticised.[1]
